summary: Defines IS-IS extensions that let a Path Computation Client automatically find Path Computation Elements and learn their capabilities. It parallels the OSPF extensions in RFC 5088. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: Routers needing help planning routes can ask around who the planners are. This lets IS-IS announce which servers are route planners and what they are good at.

questions: how to discover pce with is-is
what is a path computation element
subtitle: How IS-IS routers announce which servers can compute paths, and what kinds of paths each one can handle.

tldr.problem: A Path Computation Client needs to find Path Computation Elements, and learn enough about each one to choose between them, without manual configuration.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a PCED sub-TLV carried in the IS-IS Router Capability TLV. It holds the PCE address, the path scopes it supports with preferences, the domains it knows, and optional capability flags, and it is flooded with normal IS-IS advertisements.
tldr.outcome: PCCs can learn about new, failed or changed PCEs from IS-IS itself. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 9353.

today: RFC 5089 is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 9353. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Finding Path Computation Elements
sections.content:
In the PCE architecture of RFC 4655, a Path Computation Client (PCC) asks a Path Computation Element (PCE) to compute paths for MPLS and GMPLS traffic engineered label switched paths (TE LSPs). A network may contain many PCEs with different capabilities, so a PCC needs a way to discover them automatically, and to notice new PCEs, failed PCEs and changed information. Requirements are in RFC 4674.

When PCCs are routers in the IGP and PCEs are routers or servers also taking part in it, the RFC notes that IGP advertisements are an effective discovery mechanism. This document does that for IS-IS, using the generic router capability advertisement of RFC 4971. The PCE selection algorithm a PCC applies is out of scope, and so is discovery across AS boundaries, which is left for further study.
sections.eli5: If you need someone to plan a trip for you, you want a list of who is available and what they are good at. This document lets routers share that list.

sections.title: What a PCE Announces and Where It Floods
sections.content:
The discovery information has five parts: the PCE location (an IPv4 and/or IPv6 address, preferably one that is always reachable), its path computation scope (intra-layer, inter-area, inter-AS or inter-layer), the PCE-Domains it can see, the neighbor PCE-Domains toward which it can compute paths, and a set of communication and path computation capabilities.

This information is fairly static. It changes with configuration updates, activation, deactivation or failure, so it is not expected to change often.

The flooding scope can be a single L1 area, an L1 area plus the L2 sub-domain, or the entire IS-IS routing domain.
sections.eli5: Each planner puts up a small card saying where to find it, what trips it can plan, and what else it can do. The card does not change much, so it does not need to be reposted often.

sections.title: The PCED Sub-TLV and Its Parts
sections.content:
The PCED sub-TLV has type 5 and carries an unordered set of sub-TLVs. They use the same format as RFC 3784: 1 octet of type, 1 octet of length, then the value. It is carried inside the IS-IS Router Capability TLV of RFC 4971.

Five sub-TLVs are defined. PCE-ADDRESS and PATH-SCOPE MUST always be present. PCE-DOMAIN and NEIG-PCE-DOMAIN are optional, to help select inter-domain PCEs. PCE-CAP-FLAGS is optional and helps PCE selection. Any unrecognized sub-TLV MUST be silently ignored, and no further sub-TLVs will be added to the PCED sub-TLV in future.

PCE-ADDRESS holds one address-type octet (1 for IPv4, 2 for IPv6) and then the 4 or 16 address octets. It MAY appear twice when the PCE has both address types, but not twice for the same type; later duplicates are ignored. PCE-DOMAIN and NEIG-PCE-DOMAIN share a format: a domain-type octet (1 for an area ID, 2 for an AS number) followed by the area ID or a 32-bit AS number. A two-octet AS number is padded so that the first two octets are zero.

PCE-CAP-FLAGS is an array of 32-bit flag units, numbered from the most significant bit as bit zero. The capability registry is managed by IANA and shared with OSPF, as defined in RFC 5088.
sections.eli5: The announcement is a small labelled box with smaller boxes inside it. Two of the small boxes are always there, such as the planner's address, and the others are extras that a receiver can skip if it does not understand them.

sections.title: Path Scopes and Preferences
sections.content:
The PATH-SCOPE sub-TLV appears exactly once. Its value is a 1-octet flags field followed by a 2-octet preferences field. The flags say which kinds of TE LSP computation the PCE supports: L for intra-area, R for inter-area, S for inter-AS and Y for inter-layer. These bits are non-exclusive. Rd and Sd mark a PCE as a default PCE for inter-area or inter-AS computation, meaning it can compute a path toward any neighbor area or AS.

If both Rd and Sd are set, the PCED sub-TLV MUST NOT contain a NEIG-PCE-DOMAIN sub-TLV. When R is clear, Rd SHOULD be clear on transmission and is ignored on receipt, and the same holds for S and Sd. A NEIG-PCE-DOMAIN sub-TLV MUST be present at least once with domain-type 1 if R is set and Rd is clear, and with domain-type 2 if S is set and Sd is clear.

The preferences field holds PrefL, PrefR, PrefS and PrefY, each three bits long, where 7 is the highest preference. Operators can use them for weighted load balancing of path computation requests, for example by setting PrefS higher than PrefR on a PCE that should be preferred for inter-AS work. How a PCC uses them is a matter of local or network-wide policy.
sections.eli5: Each planner ticks boxes for the kinds of trips it can plan, and gives each kind a score from 0 to 7. A higher score means send it more of that kind of work.

sections.title: Flooding and Handling Changes
sections.content:
Procedures are inherited from RFC 4971. The S flag of the Router Capability TLV sets the scope: with S clear the PCED sub-TLV is area local, and with S set it covers the entire IS-IS routing domain. If only the L bit of PATH-SCOPE is set, the scope MUST be area local. An L1L2 node may include the PCED in both its L1 and L2 LSPs with S clear, which limits flooding to the L1 area and the L2 sub-domain.

When the PCE function is deactivated, the advertising speaker MUST originate a new IS-IS LSP without the PCED TLV. Any change of PCE state MUST be reflected as an inserted, removed or updated PCED sub-TLV. The PCE address SHOULD be reachable via some prefixes advertised by IS-IS, and the information is only current while the advertising router is itself reachable at the level of the LSP carrying it.

A change in PCED information MUST NOT trigger any SPF computation at a receiving router.
sections.eli5: The planner's card is posted on a bulletin board that covers a street, a town or a whole country. When a planner stops working, a new board is posted without its card, and nobody has to redraw the road map.

sections.title: Compatibility and Operations
sections.content:
The PCED sub-TLV introduces no interoperability issues. An IS-IS router that does not support it silently ignores it, as specified in RFC 4971. IANA assigned sub-TLV value 5 in the registry of Router Capability sub-TLVs.

The manageability section says that frequent changes to PCE information may impact IS-IS and could destabilize the network by making PCCs swap between PCEs. It requires at least a configurable limit on the rate of announcing changed parameters, control of the impact on PCCs such as rate-limiting processing of PCED sub-TLVs, and configurable triggers for a PCC to swap PCEs. A MIB module for PCE discovery is referred to as a work in progress.
sections.eli5: Routers that do not know about planners just ignore the card. And planners should not change their cards too often, or everyone keeps switching planners.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The extensions are for PCE discovery within an administrative domain, so the security of discovery relies on the security of IS-IS. Mechanisms that ensure authenticity and integrity of IS-IS LSPs and their TLVs, such as RFC 3567, can protect the PCED sub-TLV as well.

IS-IS provides no encryption mechanism, so the privacy of LSPs, and of the PCE discovery information in them, is not protected.
sections.eli5: The planner list is only as safe as the bulletin board it is posted on. The board can be checked for tampering, but anyone who can read it can see the list.

viz.caption: SUB-TLVS INSIDE THE PCED SUB-TLV (RFC 5089, SECTION 4)

items.label: PCE-ADDRESS
items.desc: Address to reach the PCE; mandatory.

items.label: PATH-SCOPE
items.desc: Supported path scopes and preferences; mandatory, length 3.

items.label: PCE-DOMAIN
items.desc: Domain where the PCE has visibility; optional.

items.label: NEIG-PCE-DOMAIN
items.desc: Neighbor domain toward which the PCE can compute paths; optional.

items.label: PCE-CAP-FLAGS
items.desc: PCE capabilities as 32-bit flag units; optional.

items.label: R
items.desc: Can act as PCE for inter-area TE LSP computation.

items.label: Rd
items.desc: Can act as a default PCE for inter-area computation.

items.label: S
items.desc: Can act as PCE for inter-AS TE LSP computation.

items.label: Sd
items.desc: Can act as a default PCE for inter-AS computation.

items.label: Y
items.desc: Can act as PCE for inter-layer TE LSP computation.
